doc.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

title: Mainstream label and the marketing of young lions
summary: Being labeled mainstream limits invitations; he criticizes record companies and critics for favoring some styles over others.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: But continuing that thought, do you ever feel that you are not included in things that you could be because you’re considered mainstream?
So it’s a double edged sword to have a label I supposed. Because you will be invited to these jazz parties, but you might not be included in —
No I think that definitely happens, yeah.
And the record companies seem to focus on a few of the “young lions” business and put their strength behind them.

Right, which is fine. I mean I don’t begrudge them. I mean I think most of the ones that get the attention are extremely talented and they’re terrific players. The only thing that bothers me a little bit is that it seems like some styles count today and others don’t, and if you look at it from a creative viewpoint it’s a little mysterious because to me it seems like if the young guy plays like Freddie Hubbard or Woody Shaw, that’s taken seriously. Whereas if you listen to Buck Clayton and Louis Armstrong that’s not. To me, they’re both equal repertoire at this point. And one of the things that troubles me, I mean it used to be a basic tenet of jazz that to be a major player you really had to say something different that was really, you know, almost more than just having a personal style. The great players would influence all musicians on all instruments because they were really taking it in a new direction. And now it seems like the marketing has kind of taken over and so they want to sell something. In order to sell something you have to sell something that people are kind of already familiar with. So much to do is made about guys who are very talented, but a kind of, you know, treading on ground that’s been pretty well cultivated before, and it’s done quite well and everything and that’s fine, but I guess, and I understand all the dynamics of it from the record companies, the magazines, etcetera. I guess if I have a criticism maybe it’s to the critics, who should be saying well this is fine but trying to encourage some of the more creative things going on. And that I find a little lacking these days.
